ai.literal: At the place where it is effective, he who restrains anger is he who restrains. At the place where it is not, if restrained, what? If not restrained, what?
ai.translation: He who restrains his anger where it can be effective is the true restrainer. Where it cannot be effective, what does it matter whether he restrains it or not?
ai.modern: தன் சினம் பலிக்கும் இடத்தில் அதைக் கட்டுப்படுத்துபவனே உண்மையாகவே சினத்தைக் கட்டுப்படுத்துபவன் ஆவான். சினம் பலிக்காத இடத்தில், அதைக் கட்டுப்படுத்தினால் என்ன, கட்டுப்படுத்தாவிட்டால் என்ன?
ai.explanation: This couplet defines true restraint of anger by examining the power dynamic between people. The word 'செல்லிடத்து' (where it goes or is effective) refers to situations where a person has the power to act on their anger, such as against the weak. Restraining anger in such situations is the only genuine restraint. In contrast, 'அல்லிடத்து' (where it is not effective) refers to situations where one is powerless. In those cases, holding back anger is merely a necessity, and whether one restrains it or not makes no practical difference.

ai.literal: Ineffective in place anger is evil; effective in place even, there is not than that evil other.
ai.translation: Anger is bad when directed at those against whom it is powerless. Even when it has the power to act, there is no greater evil than anger.
ai.modern: தன் அதிகாரம் செல்லாத இடத்தில் கோபம் கொள்வது தீமையானது. அதிகாரம் செல்லும் இடத்திலும் கூட, அக்கோபத்தை விடத் தீமையானவை வேறு எதுவும் இல்லை.
ai.explanation: This couplet evaluates anger based on the power dynamic between the angry person and their target. When directed at someone stronger, where it cannot take effect, anger is harmful because it invites retaliation and ruin. Yet, even when directed at someone weaker, where it can take effect, there is no evil worse than anger itself, as it destroys one's own peace and character. The verb 'செல்' (to go) is used here in the specific sense of being effective or having power over a situation.

ai.literal: Forgetting anger towards anyone; evil things arising from it will come.
ai.translation: Forget anger towards anyone, for all evil things arise from it.
ai.modern: யாரிடத்திலும் கோபம் கொள்வதை மறந்துவிட வேண்டும்; ஏனெனில் தீமையான செயல்கள் அனைத்தும் அந்தக் கோபத்தாலேயே உண்டாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet advises completely abandoning anger, regardless of who the target might be. The word 'மறத்தல்' literally means 'forgetting', but here it functions as a strong injunction to let go of anger entirely. 'யார்மாட்டும்' emphasizes that anger is destructive whether directed at the strong or the weak. The reason given is that 'தீய' (evil things) naturally arise and come from anger itself. Therefore, avoiding anger is the only way to prevent the birth of further evils.

ai.literal: Smile and joy destroying, than anger, enemies are there other?
ai.translation: Are there any enemies other than anger, which destroys both a person's smile and their joy?
ai.modern: ஒருவருடைய முகமலர்ச்சியையும் மன மகிழ்ச்சியையும் கொன்றழிக்கின்ற சினத்தை விட வேறு பகையும் உண்டோ?
ai.explanation: The couplet asks a rhetorical question to emphasize the destructive nature of anger. It identifies a person's outward smile ('நகை') and inward joy ('உவகை') as the first victims of their own anger. Because anger destroys these fundamental sources of human happiness, the text concludes that there is no greater enemy to a person than their own wrath.

ai.literal: Oneself oneself if protects, anger let guard; if not guarded, oneself indeed will kill anger.
ai.translation: If you wish to protect yourself, guard against anger. If you do not guard against it, that anger will kill you.
ai.modern: ஒருவன் தன்னைத் தான் காத்துக்கொள்ள விரும்பினால், அவன் தன் சினத்தைக் கட்டுப்படுத்த வேண்டும். அப்படிச் சினத்தைக் காக்கவில்லை என்றால், அந்தச் சினமே அவனை அழித்துவிடும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet establishes a direct link between self-preservation and the control of anger. The word 'காக்கின்' (if one protects) sets up a condition: true self-protection requires restraining one's own wrath. If a person fails to guard against it ('காவாக்கால்'), the very anger they harbor becomes a destructive force. Ultimately, the anger turns inward and destroys the person who holds it, emphasized by 'தன்னையே கொல்லும்' (will kill oneself indeed).

ai.literal: The killer of those who joined called anger, will burn the safe raft called kin.
ai.translation: The killer called anger destroys the very person who harbors it. It will also burn down the safe raft known as one's family and friends.
ai.modern: சினம் என்னும் தீ தன்னைச் சேர்ந்தவர்களையே அழிப்பதோடு, சுற்றம் என்று சொல்லப்படும் பாதுகாப்பான தெப்பத்தையும் சுட்டழித்துவிடும்.
ai.explanation: Anger is described as a destructive force that first ruins the person who holds onto it. Beyond destroying the individual, it also burns away their vital support system. The poet uses the metaphor of a safe raft to represent family and friends, showing that anger leaves a person completely isolated and defenseless in the sea of life.

ai.literal: Anger as a worthy thing having considered, he who holds [it], [his] ruin; on the ground he who struck, [his] hand will not fail [to be hurt], it is like that.
ai.translation: The ruin of a man who holds onto anger as a worthy principle is as certain as the pain of a hand that strikes the hard ground.
ai.modern: சினத்தை ஒரு சிறந்த பொருளாகக் கருதி மனத்துள் கொள்பவனுக்கு அழிவு நிச்சயம். அது நிலத்தில் ஓங்கி அடித்தவனின் கைக்கு வலி தப்பாததைப் போன்றது.
ai.explanation: This couplet illustrates the inevitable self-destruction caused by holding onto anger. The word 'பொருள்' here means a thing of value or a guiding principle; treating anger as something useful is a grave mistake. Just as a person who strikes the hard ground cannot escape hurting their own hand, a person who harbors anger cannot escape their own ruin. The vivid image of striking the earth emphasizes that the damage is immediate, self-inflicted, and absolutely certain.

ai.literal: Cluster fire plunging like painful things even if done, if possible non-anger is good.
ai.translation: Even if someone inflicts pain as severe as plunging you into a blazing fire, it is good if you can manage not to get angry.
ai.modern: பல சுடர்களை உடைய நெருப்பில் விழுவது போன்ற துன்பங்களை ஒருவர் செய்தாலும், முடிந்தால் அவர் மேல் கோபம் கொள்ளாமல் இருப்பது நல்லது.
ai.explanation: The couplet compares severe harm caused by others to being thrown into a blazing, multi-flamed fire (இணர் எரி). Even when facing such extreme and painful provocation (இன்னா செயினும்), the text advises restraint. The word 'புணரின்' means 'if it is possible' or 'if one can manage it', acknowledging how difficult it is to control anger in such situations. Ultimately, maintaining non-anger (வெகுளாமை) under such intense trials is declared to be a true good (நன்று).

ai.literal: That which was thought all immediately he will attain, with the mind he will not think anger if.
ai.translation: If a person does not let anger enter even his thoughts, he will instantly attain everything he has wished for.
ai.modern: ஒருவன் தன் மனத்தால் கூடச் சினத்தை நினைக்கமாட்டான் என்றால், அவன் நினைத்ததை எல்லாம் உடனே அடைவான்.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes the power of absolute self-control over anger. If a person can prevent anger from even entering their mind, they achieve a state of mental clarity and strength. In this state, whatever they wish for or set their mind to will be attained immediately. The word 'உள்ளத்தால்' stresses that avoiding anger is not just an outward show, but a deep internal purity.

ai.literal: Those who transgress dead people are like; anger those who renounced ascetics equal.
ai.translation: Those who transgress through anger are like the dead. Those who have renounced anger are equal to ascetics who have renounced everything.
ai.modern: சினத்தால் நன்னடத்தை வரம்பை மீறியவர்கள் இறந்தவர்களுக்கு ஒப்பானவர்கள். சினத்தை விட்டொழித்தவர்கள் முற்றும் துறந்த முனிவர்களுக்கு ஒப்பானவர்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet contrasts those who yield to anger with those who conquer it. The word 'இறந்தார்' is used twice: first to mean those who transgress the limits of good conduct through anger, and second to mean the dead, implying that angry people are as good as dead. Similarly, 'துறந்தார்' is used twice: first for those who have renounced anger, and second for ascetics who have renounced the world, showing that conquering anger is as great as ultimate renunciation.
